statement: For g:[a,b]→I differentiable with continuous derivative g', where I⊂ℝ is an interval, and f:I→ℝ continuous, the substitution rule holds: ∫_a^b f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u) du. Equivalently, setting u = g(x) so that du = g'(x) dx, an integral in x is transformed into an integral in u with the limits replaced by g(a) and g(b).

symbols.meaning: continuous integrand defined on interval I
differentiable function with continuous derivative, maps [a,b] into I
antiderivative of f on I, i.e. F' = f

steps.text: Since f is continuous on I, it has an antiderivative F on I, so F'(u) = f(u) for u in I. Form the composite function F∘g on [a,b].
Since g is differentiable, the chain rule applied to F∘g gives (F∘g)'(x) = F'(g(x))·g'(x) = f(g(x))·g'(x), using F' = f.
Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to (F∘g)' on [a,b]: ∫_a^b f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = ∫_a^b (F∘g)'(x) dx = (F∘g)(b) − (F∘g)(a) = F(g(b)) − F(g(a)).
Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus again, this time to F' = f over the interval with endpoints g(a) and g(b): F(g(b)) − F(g(a)) = ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} F'(u) du = ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u) du.

Combine steps 3 and 4: ∫_a^b f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u) du. This is the substitution rule; in Leibniz notation it is reached heuristically by writing u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx and replacing the x-limits a, b with the u-limits g(a), g(b).

assumptions.assumption: g is differentiable on [a,b] with continuous derivative g'.
assumptions.breaks_when: g' fails to exist or is discontinuous at some point of [a,b]; the proof step (F∘g)'(x) = f(g(x))·g'(x) and the fundamental-theorem application to (F∘g)' then no longer apply.

assumptions.assumption: f is continuous on the interval I containing the range of g.
assumptions.breaks_when: f is discontinuous somewhere on g([a,b]); then f may not have an antiderivative F on I, so step 1 fails.

failure_modes.mode: Substitution produces an integral that is not actually simpler or not of a form permitting the method.
failure_modes.signature: After substituting u = g(x), the resulting integrand ∫ f(u) du still cannot be evaluated in closed form, or du = g'(x) dx cannot be matched against the rest of the integrand.
failure_modes.cause: The chosen g does not make the integrand's non-g'(x) factor expressible purely in terms of u = g(x); the source notes explicitly that 'not all integrals are of a form that permits its use.'

failure_modes.mode: Forgetting to transform the limits of integration.
failure_modes.signature: Evaluating ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u) du using the original x-limits a, b instead of g(a), g(b).
failure_modes.cause: The definite-integral form of the rule requires replacing the limits (per the statement 'the limits of integration must also be adjusted'), which is skipped if one evaluates the antiderivative in u without converting back to x or updating the bounds.
